title: RAG & Memory Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation, embeddings and vector search, long-term memory architectures for agents.
html:
A pretrained model's knowledge is parametric: facts are compressed into weights during pretraining and are thereafter frozen, undocumented and unattributable. Retrieval-augmented generation attacks all three properties at once by moving some of the knowledge out of the weights and into a searchable store that is read at inference time. The idea is old — Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, named it and trained retriever and generator jointly — but the modern practice has drifted far from that paper: almost nobody trains the retriever end-to-end any more, and RAG in 2025 usually means an engineering pipeline bolted in front of a frozen API model.

What retrieval actually buys

It is worth being precise about the problems RAG solves, because each one implies different design pressure and several of them are not about knowledge at all.

Problem with parametric knowledgeWhat retrieval changes
Frozen at the pretraining cutoffThe store is updated by writing a document, not by retraining
Updating a fact requires fine-tuning or model editing, both unreliableDelete and reinsert a chunk; the change is exact and immediate
No provenance — the model cannot say where a fact came fromRetrieved chunks carry document IDs, so answers can be cited and audited
Private or proprietary corpora were never in pretrainingCompany documents become usable without exposing them to a training run
Rare, long-tail facts are memorized poorly or not at allLong-tail facts are as retrievable as common ones — the index does not have a frequency prior
Access control is impossible — weights cannot enforce per-user permissionsFilter the index by the caller's permissions before generation ever sees the text

The access-control and provenance properties are underrated and often decisive. In an enterprise deployment the reason to use retrieval is frequently not that the model lacks the knowledge but that the deployment must be able to answer “which document did that come from” and must not surface a document the caller is not cleared to read. No amount of fine-tuning gives you either. This is why RAG persists in production even where a long-context model could technically hold the corpus.

Retrieval does not fix reasoning. A model that cannot do multi-step arithmetic does not become able to when handed the right passage. Retrieval addresses a knowledge deficit, and it is a common and expensive category error to reach for RAG when the failure is actually in the model's reasoning, formatting, or instruction-following — those are post-training problems (sections 7 and 8), not retrieval problems.

The pipeline, mechanically

A production RAG system is a chain of five or six stages, each with its own failure mode. The end-to-end quality is roughly the product of the stage qualities, which is why debugging RAG means instrumenting every stage rather than looking at final answers.

documents
  -> chunking            split into retrievable units
  -> embedding           chunk -> dense vector, done once, offline
  -> indexing            build an ANN structure over the vectors
--- query time ---
query
  -> query transform     rewrite / expand / decompose (optional)
  -> retrieval           ANN search, top-k candidates (k ~ 50-200)
  -> reranking           cross-encoder rescoring, keep top-n (n ~ 3-10)
  -> prompt assembly     chunks + instructions + question
  -> generation          the LLM conditions on the assembled context
The two RAG lanes: an offline path that chunks and embeds the corpus into a vector index, and an online path that embeds the query, retrieves the nearest chunks from that same index, and pastes them into the prompt.

Chunking is the stage people under-think and it is genuinely hard. The unit you index is the unit you retrieve, and it must satisfy two conflicting constraints. It must be small enough that its embedding is a faithful summary — a single vector for a 4000-token chapter averages away everything specific, which is the same destructive-averaging argument that motivates multi-head attention in section 1. It must also be large enough to be self-contained, because a chunk that says “this reduced latency by 40%” without naming what this is will be retrieved and then mislead the generator. Typical settings land at 200–800 tokens with 10–20% overlap; the overlap exists specifically to keep a fact that straddles a boundary intact in at least one chunk. Overlap costs index size and introduces near-duplicate retrievals that eat your top-k budget.

Structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size chunking when structure exists. Splitting on document headings, function boundaries in code, or semantic shifts detected by embedding-distance between adjacent sentences all outperform naive character windows. A common and cheap improvement is contextual augmentation: prepend the document title and section path to each chunk before embedding, so the chunk's vector inherits the topical context that its raw text lost. A related trick is to decouple the retrieved unit from the embedded unit — embed a small precise chunk, but return its surrounding parent section to the generator.

Embedding models and the dual-encoder design

Dense retrieval rests on a bi-encoder (equivalently, dual-encoder): one network maps a query to a vector, another (usually the same weights) maps a passage to a vector, and relevance is approximated by an inner product or cosine similarity in that shared space.

score(q, d) = cos( E(q), E(d) )     # E is a single encoder, or a pair

# The whole point: E(d) is computed ONCE, offline, for every d.
# At query time you embed q and do a vector search. Cost is
# independent of corpus size except through the index.

The architectural constraint is that query and document never see each other. Every interaction between them is squeezed through a single dot product between two independently-computed vectors. That is what makes the corpus precomputable and search sublinear, and it is also the ceiling on accuracy — no amount of encoder quality lets a bi-encoder model a term-level interaction it never got to compute.

Training is contrastive. Given a query and its known-relevant passage, the objective raises their similarity and lowers similarity to negatives, typically with an InfoNCE loss over a batch where other examples' passages serve as in-batch negatives:

L = -log( exp(sim(q, d+)/T) / sum_j exp(sim(q, d_j)/T) )
#   d+ is the positive; d_j ranges over d+ and all negatives
#   T is a temperature; larger batches = more negatives = better

Hard negatives are where retrieval quality is actually won. Random in-batch negatives are trivially separable, so the model learns only coarse topicality. Mining negatives that a current retriever ranks highly but that are in fact irrelevant — then retraining against them — is the standard recipe, iterated. Karpukhin et al. (2020), Dense Passage Retrieval, established the modern form of this; later work (the E5, GTE and BGE families among others) scaled it with large synthetic and weakly-supervised corpora.

Practical selection notes. Embedding models are domain-sensitive — a model trained on web text and QA pairs may do poorly on legal citations, chemical nomenclature or code, and the ranking on a public leaderboard frequently does not survive contact with a specific corpus. Dimensionality trades index cost against fidelity, and Matryoshka-style training (Kusupati et al., 2022, Matryoshka Representation Learning) produces embeddings whose leading dimensions are usable alone, letting one model serve several dimension budgets. Symmetric similarity (sentence-to-sentence) and asymmetric retrieval (short query to long passage) are different tasks; using a symmetric-trained model for asymmetric retrieval is a common silent quality loss, which is why many models require an instruction prefix distinguishing the two.

Vector indexing and approximate nearest neighbor search

Exact nearest-neighbor search over N vectors is O(N) per query with no structure to exploit — in high dimensions, the tree-based methods that work in 2-D or 3-D degrade to a full scan. Every practical system therefore uses approximate nearest neighbor search and accepts a recall below 1.0 in exchange for orders-of-magnitude speedup.

IndexMechanismBuild costMemoryNotes
Flat (brute force)Exhaustive scan, exactNoneFull vectorsCorrect baseline; fine below ~100k vectors
IVFCluster vectors (k-means); search only the nearest nprobe cellsModerate (training)Full vectorsnprobe is the direct recall/latency dial
HNSWMulti-layer navigable small-world graph; greedy descent from a coarse layerHighVectors + graph edgesBest recall/latency; memory-hungry; awkward deletes
PQ / IVF-PQSplit the vector into sub-vectors, replace each with a codebook IDModerateTiny (8–32× compression)Lossy; usually paired with an exact rescoring pass
ScaNN / anisotropic quantizationQuantization loss weighted toward preserving inner-product rankingModerateSmallOptimizes what actually matters — ranking, not reconstruction

HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin, 2016) is the default for good reason. It builds a hierarchy of proximity graphs: upper layers are sparse and let a search take large jumps across the space, lower layers are dense and refine locally. A query greedily walks toward its nearest neighbor at each layer, descending as it converges. Search is roughly logarithmic in N with excellent recall, and the parameters are legible — M (edges per node) sets graph quality and memory, efConstruction sets build quality, efSearch is the query-time recall/latency dial you tune per deployment.

Product quantization is what makes billion-scale indexes fit in RAM. A 1024-dimensional fp32 vector is 4KB; a hundred million of them is 400GB. PQ splits the vector into (say) 64 sub-vectors of 16 dimensions, k-means-clusters each subspace into 256 centroids, and stores 64 single-byte codebook IDs — 64 bytes, a 64× reduction. Distances are then computed against centroids via a precomputed lookup table. The compression is lossy, so production systems retrieve a generous candidate set from the compressed index and rescore the finalists against full-precision vectors.

The operational gotchas are metadata filtering and deletion. Filtering (“only documents this user can read, only from 2024”) interacts badly with graph indexes: pre-filtering can disconnect the graph so the walk cannot reach valid neighbors, while post-filtering can return nothing if the entire top-k was filtered out. Deletion in HNSW is usually a tombstone plus periodic rebuild, not a real removal. Both are why a mature vector store is a real database problem and not just an ANN library.

Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval

Dense retrieval's rise created a widespread belief that lexical search is obsolete. It is not. BM25 — a term-frequency ranking function with document-length normalization and inverse-document-frequency weighting, essentially unchanged since the 1990s Okapi work of Robertson and colleagues — remains a strong baseline that dense retrievers do not uniformly beat.

PropertySparse (BM25)Dense (bi-encoder)
Matches onExact terms, weighted by raritySemantic proximity in embedding space
Synonyms / paraphraseFails — no term overlap, no matchHandles well; this is the main win
Rare identifiers (error codes, SKUs, names)Excellent — high IDF makes them decisiveOften poor — unseen tokens embed uninformatively
Out-of-domain corpusRobust; nothing was trainedDegrades, sometimes sharply
New documentsIndex immediatelyMust embed first; re-embed everything if the model changes
CostVery cheap; mature inverted-index infrastructureGPU embedding cost plus vector-index memory
ExplainabilityYou can point at the matched termsOpaque — a similarity score with no decomposition

The BEIR benchmark (Thakur et al., 2021) is the standard evidence. Evaluating retrievers zero-shot across many heterogeneous domains, it found that dense retrievers trained on one distribution frequently underperformed BM25 when moved to another — the in-domain wins did not generalize. This result has aged well and is the empirical reason hybrid retrieval became standard practice rather than a hedge.

Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses the rankings. The scores are not comparable — BM25 is unbounded, cosine similarity sits in [-1, 1] — so the robust default is reciprocal rank fusion, which discards the scores entirely and combines ranks:

RRF(d) = sum over retrievers r of  1 / (k + rank_r(d))
# k ~ 60 by convention; damps the influence of any single
# retriever's top hit and needs no score calibration

Learned sparse retrieval is the third option and deserves more attention than it gets. Models in the SPLADE family (Formal et al., 2021) produce a sparse vector over the vocabulary rather than a dense one: the model expands a query with related terms and weights them, so you get semantic matching while keeping an inverted index and its exact-match strength. It sits genuinely between the two columns above rather than being a compromise between them.

Reranking and the cross-encoder

The bi-encoder's precomputability constraint — query and document never interact — can be lifted if you are willing to pay per pair. A cross-encoder concatenates query and passage into one sequence and runs a full transformer over them, letting every query token attend to every passage token, then emits a single relevance score.

bi-encoder:     score = cos( E(q), E(d) )        # 1 encode of q, d precomputed
cross-encoder:  score = f( Encoder([q ; SEP ; d]) )  # 1 full forward pass PER PAIR

The accuracy gain is large and the cost is prohibitive at corpus scale. Cross-encoders capture term-level interactions a dot product cannot represent, and consistently top retrieval leaderboards. But scoring a query against 10 million documents means 10 million forward passes, and nothing can be precomputed because the score depends on the pair. Hence the retrieve-then-rerank cascade: a cheap retriever with high recall produces 50–200 candidates, and the expensive scorer reorders only those. You are buying precision at the top of the list with a bounded amount of compute.

The cascade's ceiling is the first stage's recall. A reranker can only reorder what it was given — if the correct passage was not in the retrieved candidate set, no reranker recovers it. This is the argument for setting first-stage k generously and for hybrid first-stage retrieval: the first stage should be tuned for recall, the second for precision, and tuning both for the same thing wastes the cascade.

Late interaction is the intermediate design. ColBERT (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020) keeps a per-token embedding for every document token and scores by summing, over query tokens, the maximum similarity to any document token. This preserves much of the cross-encoder's term-level sensitivity while still precomputing document representations — at the cost of an index one to two orders of magnitude larger, which is why it is common in research and less common in production.

Query transformation

The query the user typed is frequently not the query that retrieves well. The document uses different vocabulary; the question is conversational and elliptical; or it requires facts from two documents that no single query reaches. Query transformation spends an extra LLM call to fix this before retrieval runs.

TechniqueWhat it doesWhen it helps
Query rewritingResolve pronouns and ellipsis against conversation history into a standalone queryMulti-turn chat — nearly mandatory; “what about the second one?” retrieves nothing
Multi-queryGenerate several paraphrases, retrieve for each, fuse the resultsVocabulary mismatch; cheap recall insurance
DecompositionSplit a compound question into sub-questions retrieved separatelyMulti-hop questions no single query can satisfy
HyDEHave the LLM hallucinate a plausible answer, embed that, retrieve against itQuery/document asymmetry — a fake answer looks more like a real passage than a question does
Step-back promptingAsk a more general question first, retrieve background, then the specific oneQuestions needing conceptual grounding before specifics

HyDE (Gao et al., 2022, Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels) is the cleverest of these and the most misread. Its premise is that a question and its answer passage are stylistically and lexically dissimilar, so embedding the question directly is a mismatch. Generating a hypothetical answer — factually wrong is fine, nobody shows it to the user — produces text shaped like the target document, and its embedding lands nearer the right region. The hallucination is the mechanism, not a bug. The cost is an extra generation on the critical path, which matters for latency-sensitive systems.

Every transformation adds latency and a failure mode of its own. A rewrite step that drops a constraint from the original question silently degrades the whole pipeline, and the damage is invisible unless you log intermediate queries. Adaptive routing — deciding per query whether retrieval is needed at all, as in the Self-RAG line of work (Asai et al., 2023) — is worth more than adding transformations unconditionally, since many queries need no retrieval and are only harmed by it.

Failure modes and evaluation

RAG fails in specific, diagnosable ways. Treating “the answer was wrong” as one bucket makes the system undebuggable.

FailureSymptomWhere to fix
Retrieval missCorrect passage never enters the candidate setChunking, embedding model, hybrid retrieval, larger first-stage k
Distractor passagesPlausible-but-irrelevant chunks retrieved; the model uses themReranking, relevance thresholding, fewer chunks in context
Chunk-boundary lossA fact split across chunks; neither half is retrievable or usableOverlap, structure-aware splitting, parent-document expansion
Positional effectsRight passage retrieved but buried mid-context and ignoredOrder by rank; put the strongest chunk first or last
Context/parametric conflictRetrieved text contradicts memorized knowledge; model picks the wrong onePrompt instructions on source precedence; conflict-aware training
Unsupported synthesisAnswer blends retrieved and invented content, cited as if all sourcedFaithfulness scoring, sentence-level attribution checks

Distractors do active harm, not neutral harm. The intuition that irrelevant context is merely ignored is wrong: Shi et al. (2023), Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context, showed measurable accuracy drops from adding irrelevant material. So retrieving more is not safely conservative — raising k past the point where precision falls makes answers worse, and the optimum is often surprisingly small, in the range of three to five well-chosen chunks. Positional effects compound this: Liu et al. (2023), Lost in the Middle, documented a U-shaped accuracy curve in which evidence at the start or end of a long context is used far more reliably than evidence in the middle.

Evaluation must be split by stage, and the two halves do not imply each other. Retrieval is measured with the classical IR metrics — recall@k (is the gold passage anywhere in the top k), MRR (mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant hit), and nDCG@k (graded relevance with a position discount). Generation is measured on faithfulness (is every claim supported by the retrieved context), answer relevance, and correctness against a reference, usually with an LLM judge and its known biases (section 13).

Optimizing recall@k does not reliably improve answers, and this is the central evaluation trap. Raising k mechanically raises recall while lowering precision, so retrieval metrics improve as answer quality declines — the two move in opposite directions across exactly the range practitioners tune. Retrieval metrics also treat all misses alike, when in practice a near-miss the model can still reason from and a topically-adjacent distractor that misleads it have opposite consequences. Track both halves and treat end-to-end answer quality as the objective; retrieval metrics are diagnostics for why the end-to-end number moved, not targets in themselves.

Long context versus retrieval

Once a model accepts hundreds of thousands of tokens, the obvious question is whether to keep a retrieval pipeline at all rather than paste in the documents. As of the early-2025 literature this is genuinely contested, and the honest position is that long context shifts the tradeoff rather than settling it.

ConsiderationLong contextRetrieval
Corpus scaleBounded by the window — useless for a 50GB corpusScales to billions of chunks
Cost per queryPay attention cost over everything, every callPay only for the chunks used
LatencyPrefill over a huge prompt dominates TTFT (section 22)Retrieval adds tens of ms; the prompt stays small
FreshnessWhatever you pasted; caching complicates updatesIndex write is immediate
AttributionModel must self-report which part it usedChunk IDs are known before generation
Access controlAll-or-nothing on the pasted materialFilter at retrieval, per caller
Reasoning over the whole corpusStrong — genuinely global questions workWeak — “summarize all 400 documents” is not a retrieval query

Where long context genuinely wins is the class of queries retrieval cannot express. Aggregation and global-structure questions — comparing two long documents, tracking a theme across a whole book, summarizing everything — have no top-k formulation, because the answer depends on all of the material rather than a retrievable subset. Long context also removes an entire category of chunking and boundary bugs, which is a real engineering saving.

Where retrieval wins is scale, cost and latency, and these do not go away. Attention cost over a long prompt is real even with the efficiency work of section 6, prefill over 500k tokens is seconds of latency and a large bill, and no window holds an enterprise corpus. The practical synthesis is a hybrid that most production systems have converged on: retrieve generously, then use the long window to hold many more candidates than a short-context system could, letting the model do the final selection. Long context makes retrieval less precise-critical — it does not remove it. Note also that reported long-context evaluations are frequently needle-in-a-haystack tests, which measure lookup rather than reasoning over dispersed evidence, and models look considerably better on the former than the latter.

Agent memory architectures

Memory for an agent (section 16) is a superset of RAG: the store is written by the agent itself during operation, not only read from a static corpus, which introduces write policy, staleness and error accumulation as new problems. The useful decomposition borrows loosely from cognitive terminology.

Memory typeSubstrateContentsFailure mode
WorkingThe context window itselfCurrent task, recent turns, live tool resultsOverflow; positional dilution
EpisodicVector or event storePast interactions, retrieved by similarity or recencyRetrieving a superseded episode as current
SemanticKey-value or graph storeDistilled facts — preferences, entities, learned constraintsStale or contradictory facts never reconciled
ProceduralPrompts, skills, tool definitionsHow to perform recurring tasksDrift from the actual environment
ArchivalFiles, databases, external systemsEverything, addressed explicitly by the agentAgent never thinks to look

Compaction is the mechanism that makes long-running agents possible. When the context approaches its limit, older turns are summarized into a compact state and the raw turns are dropped. The design questions are what must survive verbatim (identifiers, file paths, exact error strings, the user's original instruction — all of which paraphrase badly) versus what can be compressed to a sentence, and how to avoid compounding error, since each compaction summarizes a previous summary and small distortions accumulate over many rounds. Anchoring every compaction to the original task statement rather than to the previous summary alone limits the drift.

The MemGPT line of work (Packer et al., 2023) framed this as an operating-system analogy — the context window is physical memory, external stores are disk, and the agent issues its own paging calls to move information between them. The framing is useful because it makes explicit that eviction policy is a design decision the system must own. Whether memory writes should be agent-controlled (the model decides what to remember, flexible but unreliable) or system-controlled (deterministic extraction rules, predictable but rigid) remains unsettled; production systems commonly do both, with system rules for structured facts and agent-issued writes for everything else.

Retrieval-by-similarity is the wrong default for memory. Unlike a document corpus, agent memory has time structure and supersession: the user's stated preference from last week is outranked by the correction from this morning, and cosine similarity has no way to know that. Practical memory retrieval blends similarity with recency and an importance score, and needs an explicit invalidation path for facts that have been overwritten — otherwise the agent confidently retrieves a fact it was already told is wrong.

Gotcha The most expensive mistake in RAG is treating embedding search as strictly superior to lexical search and skipping BM25 entirely. Dense retrieval's advantage is paraphrase and synonymy; its weakness is exactly the queries enterprise systems get most — an error code, a part number, a person's name, an internal acronym. A rare identifier has enormous IDF and BM25 nails it, while an embedding model that never saw the token in training maps it somewhere uninformative and returns topically-plausible garbage. Compounding this, the BEIR results (Thakur et al., 2021) showed dense retrievers underperforming BM25 out-of-domain across many datasets, and your corpus is out-of-domain for any off-the-shelf embedding model. Build BM25 first, measure it, and treat it as the number dense retrieval must beat rather than as a legacy fallback — then run both and fuse, which beats either alone in most published comparisons. The corollary is architectural: a “vector database” is a component of a retrieval system, not the system, and a design that starts by choosing one has already skipped the decisions that determine whether retrieval works.
